questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Area Bounded Between a Curve and the Y-Axis by First Rewriting the Function
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14059137/assets/9e19c1cd8bca76f1eec39acfa1b09c0f08b67faea5ddce8325e093923d21d394.png)

Find the area bounded between the curve $y=\sqrt[3]{x+1},$ the $y$-axis and the lines $y=0$ and $y=1,$ as shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make $x$ the subject:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt[3]{x+1} \\ {y}^{3} & =x+1 \\ x & ={y}^{3}-1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the area, we compute the corresponding definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{c}^{d}x(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({y}^{3}-1)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y-{\int }_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\frac{{y}^{4}}{4}|}_{0}^{1}-y{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{1}{4}-0)-(1-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}-1 \\  & =-\frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

We obtained a negative number because the region lies to the left of the $y$-axis. So the area that we want is $|-\frac{3}{4}|=\frac{3}{4}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Finite Area Bounded Between a Curve and the Y-Axis
questions.problem: Find the area of the closed region between the curve $x=16{y}^{4}-1$ and the $y$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find $y$-intercepts of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}16{y}^{4}-1 & =0 \\ 16{y}^{4} & =1 \\ {y}^{4} & =\frac{1}{16} \\ y & =\pm \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we draw a sketch of the region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14059137/assets/c1e092dd6302bb5948c6452e43b093fc3a531132580c1bb1e42fbe846152f63c.png)

We want to find the area between the curve $x=16{y}^{4}-1$ and the $y$-axis from $y=-\frac{1}{2}$ to $y=\frac{1}{2}.$ To find the area, we compute the corresponding definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{c}^{d}x(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1/2}^{1/2}(16{y}^{4}-1)\,\text{d}y \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{1/2}(16{y}^{4}-1)\,\text{d}y \\  & =32{\int }_{0}^{1/2}{y}^{4}\,\text{d}y-2{\int }_{0}^{1/2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =32\cdot {\frac{{y}^{5}}{5}|}_{0}^{1/2}-2\cdot y{|}_{0}^{1/2} \\  & =\frac{32}{5}(\frac{1}{32}-0)-2(\frac{1}{2}-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}-1 \\  & =-\frac{4}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the region lies to the left of the $y$-axis, we obtained a negative number. So the area that we want is $|-\frac{4}{5}|=\frac{4}{5}.$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14059137/assets/a45999ec28d309b3be249304e9b5175f66f2b862cd7f18f2c51b3182333e9a08.png)

Find the area of the finite region bounded between the curve $x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡y$ and the $y$-axis, as shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the $y$-intercepts of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡y & =0 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡y & =0 \\ y & =\pm \frac{\pi }{2},\pm \frac{3\pi }{2},…\end{aligned}
$$

From the diagram, we see that we want to find the area between the curve $x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡y$ and the $y$-axis from $y=-\frac{\pi }{2}$ to $y=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ To find the area, we compute the corresponding definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{c}^{d}x(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}2\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,\text{d}y \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}2\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,\text{d}y \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,\text{d}y \\  & =4\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡y{|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =4(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)) \\  & =4(1-0) \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14059137/assets/cc0f19d50ccd27918d0ac005dec9a8cd27a4f104726ded0d07c71b571ad0522f.png)

Find the area between the curve $y=\sqrt{4-x}$, the $y$-axis and the lines $y=0$ and $y=1,$ as shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make $x$ the subject:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt{4-x} \\ {y}^{2} & =4-x \\ x & =4-{y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the area, we compute the corresponding definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{c}^{d}x(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(4-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}y-{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =4\cdot y{|}_{0}^{1}-{\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =4(1-0)-(\frac{1}{3}-0) \\  & =4-\frac{1}{3} \\  & =\frac{11}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14059137/assets/816b36f644f3e41d8f48bed2dd49e150d751cb13e082b6a1b9b4ad16973d3d57.png)

Find the area $A$ between the curve $y=3\sqrt{\frac{x+3}{3}}$, the $y$-axis and the lines $y=1$ and $y=2,$ as shown above. Do not round the answer.

$A=$

{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make $x$ the subject:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =3\sqrt{\frac{x+3}{3}} \\ \frac{y}{3} & =\sqrt{\frac{x+3}{3}} \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{9} & =\frac{x+3}{3} \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{3} & =x+3 \\ x & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{3}-3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the area, we compute the corresponding definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{c}^{d}x(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(\frac{{y}^{2}}{3}-3)\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{1}^{2}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y-3{\int }_{1}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot {\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}\,|}_{1}^{2}-3\cdot y\,{|}_{1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(\frac{8}{3}-\frac{1}{3})-3(2-1) \\  & =\frac{7}{9}-3 \\  & =-\frac{20}{9}\end{aligned}
$$

We obtained a negative number because the region lies to the left of the $y$-axis. So, the area that we want is

$$
A=|-\frac{20}{9}|=\frac{20}{9}\,.
$$
